opus-5.5.text:
I think predictability is one of the most important properties of a good training setup, maybe more important than any single result. When you train a large model, each run costs a lot of compute and time, so you can't just try things randomly at full scale. What you really want is to make decisions on small experiments and be confident they will hold when you scale up.

That's why I care so much about things like scaling laws. If loss follows a smooth, predictable curve as you add compute, data, or parameters, you can fit that curve on small models and extrapolate. That turns model training from alchemy into something closer to engineering. You can ask: if I change the architecture, or the optimizer, or the data mixture, does the whole curve shift down? If yes, that's a real improvement. If it only helps at small scale and the curve bends the wrong way, you've avoided wasting a huge run.

There's also a deeper reason. Next-token prediction is about compressing the world. If a model predicts better, it has learned more structure about language, code, math, and how people reason. So predictive capability isn't just a training metric. It's a proxy for how much understanding the model has absorbed. Many downstream abilities emerge from that foundation.

Finally, predictability matters for the organization. A startup can't afford many failed big bets. If your methodology is predictable, you can plan your roadmap, allocate compute rationally, and move faster than people who rely on luck. So for me, a technique that is slightly better but unpredictable is often worse than one that is solid and scales cleanly. The goal is to find methods whose gains you can trust as you keep going up.

r001.rationale: The response says large-model runs cost substantial compute and time, so small experiments that predict scaling outcomes help avoid costly full-scale mistakes.

fable-5.1.text:
Predictive capability is really the foundation of everything we do at scale. When you're training a model that costs tens of millions of dollars, you cannot afford to run the full experiment, see what happens, and then try again. You need to know, before you commit the compute, roughly what the outcome will be.

So the way we work is that we build a kind of ladder. We run experiments at small scale, maybe one percent or even a tenth of a percent of the final compute, and we try to find laws that tell us how the loss, or some downstream capability, will change as we scale up. If those laws hold across several orders of magnitude, then we have a reasonable basis to say that a particular architecture choice, or a data mixture, or an optimizer setting, will still be the right one at the final scale.

I think a lot of people underestimate how much of this is about research methodology rather than any specific trick. In academia, you often run one experiment, get one number, and publish. But in large-scale training, a single number is almost meaningless. What matters is whether a trend is monotonic and whether it extrapolates. If an idea helps at small scale but the gap shrinks as you scale up, that idea is actually worthless for us, or even harmful, because it might distract us from things that genuinely compound.

There's also an organizational reason. When you have predictive capability, decision-making becomes much more rational. People stop arguing based on intuition or taste, and start arguing based on scaling curves. That makes a team much more efficient, because the discussion converges faster, and junior researchers can contribute as long as their experiments are well designed. Without it, every big run becomes a bet on somebody's gut feeling, and you can only afford to be wrong a very small number of times.

And honestly, I'd say predictability is also a form of understanding. If you can predict what a model will do at ten times the scale, it means you have some real model of what's going on inside, even if it's not a full theory. That's the closest thing to science we have in this field right now, and I think it's what separates teams that can keep improving from teams that just get lucky once.

astra-6.text:
I value predictive capability because it gives us a way to turn model development into a more systematic process. Before committing a lot of compute to a training run, we want to know whether a change in the data, architecture, or training objective is likely to improve the model—and whether the improvement we see at a small scale will hold at a larger scale.

If we can predict those outcomes reasonably well, we can make better decisions about where to invest. And when the results differ from our predictions, that’s useful too: it tells us there’s something about the training process we don’t yet understand. So prediction is both a practical tool for allocating resources and a test of our understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I value predictive capability because it gives us a concrete signal of whether a model has learned something useful about the world. To predict what comes next across many different contexts, it has to learn patterns, relationships, and some underlying structure—not just memorize individual examples.

Of course, prediction isn’t the whole goal. We also want models that can reason, follow instructions, and solve problems. But prediction provides a scalable training objective, and improving it can build a foundation for those broader capabilities. The important question is whether that improvement transfers to new situations and useful tasks.
